implemented_requirements.evidence: LEVELS = {"Beginner": (9, 9, 10), "Intermediate": (16, 16, 40), "Expert": (30, 16, 99)} defines the three levels and the constructor reads the selected level with self.cols, self.rows, self.mines = LEVELS[self.level_var.get()]

implemented_requirements.requirement: Player uncovers cells by clicking on them
implemented_requirements.evidence: Each button is bound with btn.bind("<Button-1>", lambda e, r=r, c=c: self.reveal(r, c)) which calls the reveal() method on left‑click.

implemented_requirements.requirement: Numbers on uncovered cells indicate how many mines are adjacent
implemented_requirements.evidence: In flood() the button text is set to str(cell.adj) when cell.adj > 0 and the colour is taken from NUM_COLORS.

implemented_requirements.requirement: If a mine is uncovered, the player loses
implemented_requirements.evidence: reveal() checks if cell.mine and calls self.game_over(cell); game_over() marks all mines and displays "BOOM! You hit a mine — Game Over".

implemented_requirements.requirement: The game displays the board with updated markings after each move
implemented_requirements.evidence: Both reveal() (via flood()) and toggle_flag() update the button configuration (bg, text, fg) immediately after each action.
Buttons are bound with btn.bind("<Button-3>", ...) and btn.bind("<Button-2>", ...) which call toggle_flag(); toggle_flag() flips cell.flag and updates the visual.
When flagged, the button shows text="⚑" with foreground FLAG_FG and background FLAG_BG, providing a distinct appearance.

critical_issues: Right‑click binding (<Button-3>) may not work on some platforms without additional configuration, but a middle‑click fallback (<Button-2>) is provided.
judge.summary: The provided main.py implements a functional Minesweeper game with three selectable difficulty levels, left‑click reveal, numbered adjacency hints, loss on mine, automatic board updates, and a flagging system with a unique visual. The code is complete and should run on a standard Python installation with Tkinter, meeting all core benchmark requirements. Minor platform‑specific concerns about right‑click handling are the only notable issue.
